zone: Bulls Tooth — the Chiwaukum Chain Lakes, Doelle Lakes and Frosty Pass
_areas_note: One peak, its own file, because Bulls Tooth is served by two trailheads that touch nothing else in this dataset. It is a Chiwaukum Mountains summit of about 6,840 ft standing directly over the upper Chiwaukum Chain Lakes in Chelan County, and it is reached either from the far end of the Icicle Creek road by the Icicle Creek trail and the Chain Lakes trail, or from the White Pine road off US 2 by Whitepine Creek, Wildhorse Creek and Frosty Pass. NOTE THE TWO NAME COLLISIONS, both of which have already misfiled this peak once. The Chain Lakes it sits above are the CHIWAUKUM Chain Lakes and are nothing to do with the Chain Lakes below La Bohn Gap in the Foss country, which is why the Foss and Necklace Valley file explicitly removed it; they are also nothing to do with the Chain Lakes on the Mount Baker highway. And the Frosty Pass on its approach is the Alpine Lakes one on Icicle Ridge, NOT the Frosty Pass in the Pasayten near Castle Peak that the Harts Pass file describes. Nothing in this file is repeated from any other: no zone file covers the Chiwaukum Chain Lakes, Doelle Lakes, the Icicle Ridge Frosty Pass, Wildhorse Creek or the White Pine road, and the lower Icicle campgrounds already written up in the Enchantments file (Bridge Creek and Eightmile) are deliberately absent here because they sit far down the road from the trailhead this peak uses. ACCESS IN 2026 IS THE FIRST THING TO CHECK, and both approaches are affected differently. A storm-damage road order running from May 2026 through the end of 2027 covers a long list of Wenatchee River district roads after the December 2025 floods, and the Icicle road specifically carries multiple landslides limiting vehicle access to the end of the road — the end of the road being exactly where the Icicle Creek trail starts. On top of that, the bridge over French Creek about a mile and a half up the Icicle Creek trail has been broken by snow load and reported unsafe, with no ford possible in high water, which severs the Chain Lakes approach outright when it is out. A large fire closure across the Lake Wenatchee and Leavenworth country ran from early August to the end of October 2026 and closed over sixty trails in the same two ranger districts; whether it reached the White Pine and Icicle roads needs confirming rather than assuming. In a bad season the Whitepine side is the one more likely to be open, and it is the longer way in.

sites.name: Chiwaukum Chain Lakes
sites.capacity: Numerous informal sites spread around the three lakes, on benches and in the timber edges. There is room for several parties and you will rarely be competing for ground — the walk in is long enough from either end that this basin stays quiet even in high summer.
sites.water: Excellent and the reason this is the camp. All three lakes hold water through the season, the inlet streams run well into late summer, and the basin is the last dependable supply before the scramble. Everything above the lakes is dry once the snow has gone, so fill completely here for summit day. Treat it; the shoreline sees steady if light use.
sites.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register and covers both day and overnight use; there is no quota, no reservation and no lottery on this side of the wilderness, which is the opposite of the Enchantments permit zone a few miles south. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the Icicle Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this wilderness, which includes every lake in this basin — carry a stove. Party size is capped, camp on existing bare ground and keep well back from the lakeshores.
sites.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Bulls Tooth and the only place a party should plan to sleep for the standard scramble. From the upper lake the route works around the shore to the base of a northwest-facing couloir filled with big white talus, climbs that to the ridge, and finishes on the summit block; most parties rappel the top section on the way down rather than reversing it, so a rope and a small rack of slings for the anchors belongs on the list even though the outing is graded as a scramble. Reaching the basin from the Icicle side is about two and a half miles and two thousand feet of climbing off the Icicle Creek trail on the Chain Lakes trail, which itself is roughly five miles and nineteen hundred feet from the junction — a full day with an overnight load. That trail was destroyed by a landslide a couple of miles south of Lake Josephine and has never been rebuilt to its old standard: it is passable on foot, it is not recommended for stock, and it is slow and vague where the slide crossed. From the west the basin is reached over Frosty Pass instead. Snow lingers in these basins into July in a normal year and the couloir holds it longer, which suits a party carrying an axe and hurts one that is not.

sites.name: Doelle Lakes
sites.capacity: Flat camping in alpine meadow threaded with talus, with room for several parties spread out. Genuinely lightly used — most people who reach the Chain Lakes stop there.
sites.water: Both lakes, reliable through the climbing season, plus snowmelt in the talus early. This is the other dependable supply in the group and the one to use if the Chain Lakes basin is occupied.
sites.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the trailhead register, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass at the Icicle Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 5,000 feet, and at this elevation the ground is thin subalpine meadow that scars for years, so pitch on bare gravel or existing sites and use a stove.
sites.notes: About one and eight tenths miles and six hundred feet above the Chain Lakes, this is the higher and more scenic option and it looks straight across at Bulls Tooth, which is the highest thing in view from here. It is the natural camp for a party that is traversing rather than going in and out — the usual line runs Icicle Creek to the Chain Lakes, over to Doelle, out past Bulls Tooth to Frosty Pass and down Wildhorse Creek to Whitepine, and this basin is the middle of it. As a base for the scramble alone it is slightly further from the couloir than the Chain Lakes are, so parties climbing the peak and returning the same way usually stay lower. The meadows here are exposed and hold weather; there is very little shelter and nights are cold well into August at this height. The connecting ground between here and the Chain Lakes is open enough to be simple in clear weather and genuinely confusing in cloud.

sites.name: Frosty Pass and the Wildhorse Creek headwaters
sites.capacity: Established ground at and just below the pass for a couple of parties, with more scattered spots in the meadows on the Wildhorse side. A crossroads rather than a destination, so expect the occasional through party in July and August and nobody at all in September.
sites.water: Snowmelt and small streams in the headwater meadows below the pass on the Wildhorse side, dependable into midsummer and thinning badly by late season. The pass itself carries nothing you can rely on. This is the last water on the western approach before the high ground, and the Icicle Ridge trail east of here is notoriously dry, so fill in the meadows rather than at the crest.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required at the White Pine trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet — this camp is above that line and there is very little to burn regardless. Camp on the existing bare sites; the meadow here is fragile and heavily walked.
sites.notes: This is the pivot of the western approach to Bulls Tooth and the last camp before the peak from that side. The Frosty and Wildhorse Creek trail runs about eleven miles and thirty-five hundred feet from the Whitepine side to the pass, where it meets the Icicle Ridge trail; from the pass the high country opens out east and north toward Lake Grace, Snowgrass Mountain, the Doelle Lakes and Bulls Tooth itself. THE TRAIL IS NOT MAINTAINED BEYOND THE PASS, so the ground linking this camp to the peak is route-finding on open high country rather than trail walking, and it is the part of the trip most likely to go wrong in poor visibility. Lake Grace lies off to the side and is the better camp of the two if you want water you can count on and shelter from the wind, at the cost of some distance. Parties doing the full traverse come over this pass in either direction, and it works as well for a party who has climbed the peak from the Chain Lakes and is walking out west as it does for one coming in. Season is roughly mid-July through early October; the north-facing approach slopes hold snow late and the pass is a cold, exposed place to be caught out.

sites.name: Whitepine Creek valley camps and the Wildhorse junction ford
sites.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the first few miles of the Whitepine Creek trail, most taking one or two tents, each with its own bit of creek. Nothing developed and no toilets.
sites.water: Whitepine Creek runs alongside for the whole of this stretch and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is the generous part of the approach, and it is worth knowing because the climb to Frosty Pass and everything above it is a different story.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the White Pine trailhead register. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal below 5,000 feet in existing rings outside a burn ban, but this is dry east-side timber and the district runs restrictions through most of the summer, so plan on a stove.
sites.notes: These exist to break the walk, and on an approach this long that matters more than it sounds. It is roughly three miles of easy valley trail from the road end to the Wildhorse Creek junction, and then six and a half miles of climbing to Frosty Pass — a poor single day with a loaded pack after the drive out from the west side. THE CRUX OF THE WHOLE APPROACH IS THE WHITEPINE CREEK FORD, a few hundred yards short of the Wildhorse junction near the ruins of the old bridge. Early in the season with snowmelt running it is a serious crossing and it is the thing that turns parties round; by late July or August it is usually a boots-on wade with a stick. Camping short of it and crossing in the morning, when the flow is at its lowest and you are fresh, is the standard tactic and the right one. Coming out, most parties walk straight through. The valley is forested and pleasant and the walking is fast, which is the argument for the Whitepine approach over the Icicle one whenever the Icicle road or the French Creek bridge is out.

sites.name: White Pine road end trailhead
sites.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the end of the road with room for a modest number of vehicles and space to sleep in one. There is no campground here, no facilities and no fee site — this is a roadhead, recorded because a party arriving late from the west side needs somewhere to be.
sites.water: Whitepine Creek is at hand and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap. Fill everything here before starting, since the good water lasts only as far as the valley and the high country above Frosty Pass has almost none.
sites.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required to park. The free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit is taken from the register here rather than arranged in advance — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book. Fire restrictions on this dry east slope are close to permanent through the summer and commonly ban all open flame including in rings.
sites.notes: The staging point for the western approach and the shorter drive from anywhere on US 2. The road leaves the highway west of Leavenworth and runs about four miles of gravel to the trailhead at roughly 2,800 feet. Sleeping here rather than pushing into the valley in the dark is worth doing, because the ford above wants daylight and a party that arrives at it tired in the evening will camp short of it anyway. THE ROAD IS THE PART TO CHECK. The December 2025 storms damaged forest roads across this whole district and a closure order covering the damaged ones runs into 2027; the Icicle road on the other side of the range carries multiple landslides limiting vehicles to the end of the road, and a large fire closure sat over the Lake Wenatchee and Leavenworth country through the autumn of 2026, shutting more than sixty trails in these two districts. Confirm the White Pine road and the Whitepine and Wildhorse trails are open before committing to the drive, and have the Icicle side as a fallback rather than an assumption, because in some seasons it has been the worse of the two.
